{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage= [[File:Sir John Meurig Thomas 20190429 130507740.jpg|210px]] | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=llqyHXtmn7s "Can Selective Catalysts Deliver Clean Technology and Sustainability?"], Sir John Meurig Thomas, 19 June 2012 | video2 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hcEPzY3lJdQ&list=PLxYMi4r71LZ7I7rAvYQxB5aCZtuDRzy8Z "Some of Tomorrow's Catalysts: Actual and Desired"], Sir John Meurig Thomas, 27 May 2015 |video3= [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=00ZV6N1UMmA&list=PLxYMi4r71LZ7I7rAvYQxB5aCZtuDRzy8Z&index=6 "Sir John Meurig Thomas discusses Humphry Davy's development of the miner's safety lamp"], The Royal Society, 31 March 2015 }}
'''Sir John Meurig Thomas''' (15 December 1932{{spnd}}13 November 2020),<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/cymrufyw/37047288|title=Y gwyddonydd, yr Athro Syr John Meurig Thomas, wedi marw|publisher=BBC Cymru Fyw|date=13 November 2020|language=cy}}</ref> also known as '''JMT''',<ref name="Jones"/> was a Welsh scientist, educator, university administrator, and historian of science primarily known for his work on [[heterogeneous catalysis]], [[solid-state chemistry]], and surface and [[materials science]].<ref name="Somorjai">{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1023/b:toca.0000003335.51469.58| title = A Tribute to John Meurig Thomas: Llongyfarchiadau ar eich penblwydd| journal = Topics in Catalysis| volume = 24| issue = 1–4| pages = 3–4| year = 2003| last1 = Somorjai | first1 = G. A. | last2 = Roberts | first2 = M. W. | s2cid = 94423899}}</ref><ref name="radioWales">{{Cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/wales/radiowales/sites/sciencecafe/updates/20111122.shtml |title=Sir John Meurig Thomas |date=22 November 2011 |publisher=BBC Radio Wales |access-date=16 November 2017}}</ref>

He was one of the founders of solid-state chemistry, starting with his work at the [[Bangor University|University of Wales, Bangor]], in 1958 when he investigated the various ways in which dislocations influence the chemical, electronic and excitonic properties of a range of solids. He was one of the first to exploit [[electron microscopy]] as a chemical tool, especially to deduce active-site reactivities from the surface topography of many minerals and crystal [[hydrate]]s. At the [[University of Aberystwyth]] (1969–1978) he elucidated the surface chemistry of diamond, clay minerals, metals and [[Intercalation (chemistry)|intercalates]] by pioneering UV and X-ray [[photoelectron spectroscopy]]. He also initiated the field of crystal engineering of organic molecules. As head of physical chemistry department at the [[University of Cambridge]] (1978–1986), then a separate department to chemistry, he used magic-angle-spinning NMR and high-resolution electron microscopy to characterize and determine the structures of [[zeolite]]s and other nanoporous [[catalyst]]s. As Fullerian Professor and Director of the [[Royal Institution]] and of the Davy–Faraday Research Laboratory, he utilized [[synchrotron radiation]] to characterize, in situ, new catalysts designed for green chemistry and clean technology.<ref name="Califano">{{cite book |last1=Califano |first1=Salvatore |title=Pathways to modern chemical physics |date=2012 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-642-28179-2 |page=52 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s-sCt4RT0bMC&pg=PA52 |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref><ref name=":0" />{{rp|6–7, 623–638}}

He was the recipient of many national and international awards; and, for his contribution to [[geochemistry]], the mineral [[meurigite]] was named in his honour.<ref name="Birch">{{cite journal |last1=Birch |first1=William D. |last2=Pring |first2=Allan |last3=Self |first3=Peter G. |last4=Gibbs |first4=Ronald B. |last5=Keck |first5=Erich |last6=Jensen |first6=Martin C. |last7=Foord |first7=Eugene E. |title=Meurigite, a new fibrous iron phosphate resembling kidwellite |journal=Mineralogical Magazine |date=5 July 2018 |volume=60 |issue=402 |pages=787–793 |doi=10.1180/minmag.1996.060.402.08 |s2cid=58928381 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237262265 |access-date=29 April 2019}}</ref> He was Master of [[Peterhouse, Cambridge|Peterhouse]], University of Cambridge (1993–2002), and was knighted in 1991 "for services to chemistry and the popularisation of science".<ref name="Symposium">{{Cite news|url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/news/symposium-honours-professor-sir-john-meurig-thomas|title=Symposium honours Professor Sir John Meurig Thomas|date=13 December 2007|work=University of Cambridge|access-date=27 April 2018|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Wright"/>

Thomas authored more than 1200 scientific articles and several books,<ref name="Harris">{{cite book |last1=Thomas |first1=John Meurig |title=The Selected Papers of Sir John Meurig Thomas |editor-last=Harris |editor-first=Kenneth D. M. |date=2017 |publisher=World Scientific |location=New Jersey |isbn=978-1-78634-187-7 |doi=10.1142/q0055 }}</ref><ref name=scopus>{{Scopus|id=23667934100}}</ref> including  ''Michael Faraday and the Royal Institution: The Genius of Man and Place'' (1991),<ref name="Faraday">{{cite book |last1=Thomas |first1=J. M. |title=Michael Faraday and the Royal Institution : the genius of man and place |date=1991 |publisher=Taylor & Francis Group |location=New York; Milton Park, Abington }}</ref>
''Principles and Practice of Heterogeneous Catalysis'' (with W. John Thomas, 1997, 2014),<ref name="Principles1997">{{cite book |last1=Thomas |first1=John Meurig |last2=Thomas |first2=W. John |title=Principles and practice of heterogeneous catalysis |url=https://archive.org/details/principlespracti0000thom |url-access=registration |date=1997 |publisher=VCH |location=Weinheim; New York |isbn=3-527-29288-8 }}</ref><ref name="Principles2014">{{cite book |last1=Thomas |first1=John Meurig |last2=Thomas |first2=W. John |title=Principles and practice of heterogeneous catalysis |date=11 December 2014 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons – VCH |isbn=978-3-527-29239-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KZfVBQAAQBAJ}}</ref> and ''Design and Applications of Single-Site Heterogeneous Catalysts: Contributions to Green Chemistry, Clean Technology and Sustainability'' (2012).<ref name="Wells"/><ref name="Catlow"/>

== Biography ==

=== Early life and education ===
Thomas was born and brought up in the [[Gwendraeth Valley]], Carmarthenshire, [[Wales]],<ref name="radioWales"/> near the mining town of [[Llanelli]],<ref name="whoswho"/> where his father and brother were miners.<ref name="McBride">{{cite book |last1=McBride |first1=J. Michael |editor-last=Harris |editor-first=Kenneth D. M. |chapter=John Thomas and Yale |page=568 |title=The selected papers of Sir John Meurig Thomas |date=2017 |publisher=World Scientific |location=New Jersey |isbn=978-1-78634-187-7 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dTBFDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA568 |access-date=29 April 2019}}</ref> He attended [[Ysgol y Gwendraeth|Gwendraeth Grammar School]].<ref name="w704">{{cite news| last=Ball | first=Philip | title=Sir John Meurig Thomas obituary | work=The Guardian | date=27 November 2020 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2020/nov/27/sir-john-meurig-thomas-obituary | access-date=5 September 2025}}</ref>

Thomas earned a BSc degree from the University College of Wales, Swansea (later [[Swansea University]]) in 1954.<ref name=":0"/>{{rp|1, 480}} He earned a PhD from Queen Mary College (later [[Queen Mary University of London]]) in 1958, working with Keble W. Sykes.<ref name="Cheetham">{{cite journal |last1=Catlow |first1=Richard |last2=Cheetham |first2=Anthony K. |title=Biography: John Meurig Thomas |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |date=November 1997 |volume=101 |issue=48 |pages=9845–9847 |doi=10.1021/jp970902v |pmid=27367524 |bibcode=1997JPCB..101.9845C }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KnEoDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA856|title=Turning Points in Solid-State, Materials and Surface Science: A Book in Celebration of the Life and Work of Sir John Meurig Thomas |editor-last=Harris |editor-first=Kenneth D. M.|editor-last2=Edwards |editor-first2=Peter P.|date=2008 |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|isbn=978-1-84755-818-3 |pages=856–857 |language=en}}</ref>{{rp|1, 796}}

===Personal life===
In 1959, Thomas married Margaret Edwards with whom he had two daughters. Margaret Thomas died in 2002.<ref name=":0" />{{rp|6–8, 864}}<ref name="Jones">{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Derry Wynn |title=Book Review: No Doubting Thomas. Turning points in solid-state, materials and surface science: a book in celebration of the life and work of Sir John Meurig Thomas, edited by Kenneth D. M. Harris and Peter P. Edwards |journal=Crystallography Reviews |date=April 2009 |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=147–150 |doi=10.1080/00343400802667749 |s2cid=97637525 }}</ref>

In April 2010, Thomas married [[Jehane Ragai]] of the [[American University in Cairo]]; the events took place in Cambridge and London.<ref name=":0" />{{rp|13}}

The recreations he lists in ''[[Who's Who (UK)|Who's Who]]'' include ancient civilisations, bird watching, and [[Welsh-language literature|Welsh literature]].<ref name="whoswho"/>

=== Early career ===
After a year's work for the [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]] as scientific officer (1957–1958), Thomas joined the Department of Chemistry at the University College of North Wales (later [[Bangor University]]) as of September 1958.<ref name=":0"/>{{rp|1}} There he rose through the ranks from Assistant Lecturer (1958), to Lecturer (1959), to Senior Lecturer (1964) and then to [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] in 1965.<ref name="Angewandte">{{cite journal |title=Sir John Meurig Thomas |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition |date=11 October 2013 |volume=52 |issue=42 |pages=10938–10940 |doi=10.1002/anie.201303486 |pmid=23728741 |last1=Thomas |first1=J. M. |bibcode=2013ACIE...5210938. }}</ref><ref name="Academia Europaea">{{cite web |title=Curriculum Vitae, Awards and Honours Professor Sir JOHN MEURIG THOMAS |url=https://www.ae-info.org/attach/User/Thomas_John_Meurig/CV/Meurig%20Thomas%20CV.pdf |website=Academia Europaea |access-date=29 April 2019}}</ref> 
Thomas demonstrated the profound influence of [[dislocations]] and other structural imperfections upon the chemical, electronic, and surface properties of solids.<ref name="Cheetham"/><ref name="Congress2001">{{cite book |title=Brisbane Australia, 1–6 JULY 2001 Congress Journal |date=2001 |publisher=World Chemistry Congress Brisbane Australia 1–6 July 2001 |chapter=Plenary Speakers |page=25 |chapter-url=https://www.raci.org.au/document/item/1173 |access-date=30 April 2019 |archive-date=26 March 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150326171639/https://www.raci.org.au/document/item/1173 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1969 Thomas became a Professor and Head of Chemistry at the [[University of Wales, Aberystwyth|University College of Wales, Aberystwyth]],<ref name="Califano"/> where he broadened his interests in solid-state, surface and materials chemistry and pioneered new techniques for the application of electron microscopy in chemistry.<ref name="Cheetham"/> In 1977 he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]].<ref name="RMAW"/>

In 1978, Thomas succeeded [[Jack Linnett]] as [[1920 Chair of Physical Chemistry|Head of the Department of Physical Chemistry]] at the [[University of Cambridge]]<ref name="Califano"/><ref name="Wright"/><ref name=":0" />{{rp|856}} (then a separate department from the Department of Chemistry, which covered Organic, Inorganic and [[Theoretical chemistry|Theoretical Chemistry]]). He also became a Professorial Fellow at [[King's College, Cambridge|King's College]], Cambridge, holding both positions until 1986.<ref name="Cheetham"/>

Thomas continued developing new techniques in solid-state and materials science, and designing and synthesising new catalysts. For example, he extended his earlier electron microscopic and surface studies of minerals and intercalates to encompass the synthesis and structural determination of [[zeolitic|zeolitic materials]] by a combination of [[solid-state NMR]], [[neutron scattering]],<ref name="Cheetham"/> and real-space imaging.<ref name="Congress2001"/><ref name="Wright"/>

=== Director of the Royal Institution ===
In 1986, Thomas succeeded Sir [[George Porter]] as Director of the [[Royal Institution|Royal Institution of Great Britain]], London.<ref name="Califano"/><ref name="James">{{cite journal |last1=James |first1=Frank A. J. L. |last2=Peers |first2=Anthony |title=Constructing Space for Science at the Royal Institution of Great Britain |journal=Physics in Perspective |date=June 2007 |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=130–185 |doi=10.1007/s00016-006-0303-5 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225700575 |access-date=29 April 2019|bibcode=2007PhP.....9..130J |s2cid=122098490 }}</ref><ref name=":0" />{{rp|xx}} He also became the holder of the [[Michael Faraday]] chair, and the Director of the Davy Faraday Research Laboratory (DFRL).<ref name=":0" />{{rp|856}} The Royal Institution was founded in 1799. Its earliest directors were [[Humphry Davy]] (1801–1825) and [[Michael Faraday]] (1825–1867). The Davy Faraday Research Laboratory opened on 22 December 1896, with funding from [[Ludwig Mond]]. It was "unique of its kind, being the only public laboratory in the world solely devoted to research in pure science".<ref name="RI2013">{{cite news |last1=Thomas |first1=Sir John Meurig |title=The Royal Institute has produced some of the most important scientific discoveries of the last century – a revival is in order |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/voices/comment/the-royal-institute-has-produced-some-of-the-most-important-scientific-discoveries-of-the-last-8536477.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220613/https://www.independent.co.uk/voices/comment/the-royal-institute-has-produced-some-of-the-most-important-scientific-discoveries-of-the-last-8536477.html |archive-date=13 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |access-date=30 April 2019 |work=The Independent |date=21 March 2013}}</ref><ref name="History">{{cite web |title=History of Research at the Ri |url=https://www.rigb.org/our-history/history-of-research |website=The Royal Institution |access-date=30 April 2019 |archive-date=14 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210414021311/https://www.rigb.org/our-history/history-of-research |url-status=dead }}</ref>

At this time, Thomas began using [[synchrotron radiation]] and devised techniques which combine [[X-ray spectroscopy]] and high-resolution [[X-Ray diffraction|X-ray diffraction]] to determine the atomic structure of the active sites of solid catalysts under operating conditions.<ref name="Califano"/><ref name=":0" />{{rp|857}} He also devised new mesoporous, microporous,<ref name="Cheetham"/> and molecular sieve catalysts.<ref name="Congress2001"/>

In 1987 the [[BBC]] televised Thomas' [[Royal Institution Christmas Lectures]] on crystals, continuing the tradition of lectures for children started by Faraday in 1825.<ref name="Wright"/><ref name="CHRISTMAS">{{cite web |title=History of the CHRISTMAS LECTURES |url=https://www.rigb.org/christmas-lectures/history |website=The Royal Institution |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref>
In 1991 Thomas published the book ''Michael Faraday and the Royal Institution: The Genius of Man and Place'', which has since been translated into Japanese (1994) and Italian (2007).<ref name=":0" />{{rp|531}}<ref name="Califano"/><ref name="Pelosi">{{cite journal |last1=Pelosi |first1=Giuseppe |title=Historical papers |journal=URSI Radio Science Bulletin |date=2017 |volume=2017 |issue=363 |pages=71–72 |doi=10.23919/URSIRSB.2017.8409432 |bibcode=2017URSB..363...71P |s2cid=246537634 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 1991, Thomas resigned as Director of the Royal Institution and the Davy Faraday Research Laboratory, to be succeeded by [[Peter Day (chemist)|Peter Day]].<ref name="Directors">{{cite web |title=Directors of the Laboratory and DFRL |url=https://www.rigb.org/our-history/history-of-research/research-directors |website=The Royal Institution |access-date=30 April 2019 |archive-date=30 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430175026/https://www.rigb.org/our-history/history-of-research/research-directors |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Frank">{{cite book |last1=James |first1=Frank A. J. L. |title=The common purposes of life : science and society at the Royal Institution of Great Britain |date=2002 |publisher=Ashgate Pub. |location=Burlington, Vt |isbn=978-0-7546-0960-5 |pages=37–38 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rzErDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT37 |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref>

=== Return to Cambridge ===
After a period as Deputy Pro-Chancellor of the [[University of Wales]] (1991–1994), Thomas returned to Cambridge in 1993 as [[Master (college)|Master]] of [[Peterhouse]], the oldest college of the university.<ref name="Cheetham"/><ref name="Views">{{cite news |title=Sir John Meurig Thomas Receives Honorary Doctorate |url=https://www.chemistryviews.org/details/ezine/2040989/Sir_John_Meurig_Thomas_Receives_Honorary_Doctorate.html |access-date=30 April 2019 |work=Chemistry Views |date=3 June 2012}}</ref> He was the first scientist to hold the position.<ref name="Wright"/>

In 1997 Thomas co-authored the text ''Principles and Practice of Heterogeneous Catalysis'' with W. John Thomas (no relation).<ref name="Principles1997"/> In 1999 John Meurig Thomas was elected Honorary Fellow of the [[Royal Academy of Engineering]]<ref name=freng>{{cite web|title=List of Fellows of the Royal Academy of Engineering|website=Royal Academy of Engineering|url=https://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows?fa=t|access-date=29 April 2019|archive-date=15 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200615185744/https://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows?fa=t|url-status=dead}}</ref> for work that "has profoundly added to the science-base of heterogeneous catalysis leading to the commercial exploitation of zeolites through engineering processes".<ref name="RSHonours">{{cite web |title=About Honours and Awards |url=https://www.cardiff.ac.uk/about/honours-and-awards/the-royal-society |website=The Royal Society |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref>

Thomas was the author of some thirty patents,<ref name="radioWales"/> some of which have made chemical processes more environmentally benign ("greener") by eliminating the use of solvents and reducing the number of manufacturing steps involved.<ref name="RMAW"/> The single-step, solvent-free catalytic synthesis of [[ethyl acetate]] that he invented is the basis of a 200,000 ton/year plant in the UK, the largest of its kind in the world.<ref name="Nanopore">{{cite journal |last1=Thomas |first1=John Meurig |last2=Raja |first2=Robert |title=Nanopore and nanoparticle catalysts |journal=The Chemical Record |date=2001 |volume=1 |issue=6 |pages=448–466 |doi=10.1002/tcr.10003 |pmid=11933251 }}</ref> He devised single-step, solvent-free processes for the production of [[caprolactam]] (the raw material for [[Nylon 6|nylon-6]]) and vitamin B<sub>3</sub> ([[Niacin (substance)|niacin]]).<ref name="Califano"/>{{rp|52}}

In 2002, Thomas stepped down from his position as Master of Peterhouse. He became Honorary Professor of Materials Science at the University of Cambridge<ref name="Wright"/> and Emeritus Professor of Chemistry at the Davy Faraday Research Laboratory of the Royal Institution.<ref name="Academia Europaea"/> He continued to be active in research at the Davy Faraday laboratory until 2006.<ref name="RSC2017">{{cite journal |last1=Thomas |first1=John Meurig |title=The RSC Faraday prize lecture of 1989 on platinum |journal=Chemical Communications |date=2017 |volume=53 |issue=66 |pages=9185–9197 |doi=10.1039/C7CC90240A |pmid=28782762 }}</ref><ref name="Zecchina">{{cite book |last1=Zecchina |first1=Adriano |last2=Califano |first2=Salvatore |title=Catalysis Science from the Onset to the Modern Days. |date=3 April 2017 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Incorporated |isbn=978-1-119-18126-2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j9pCDgAAQBAJ&pg=PT277 |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref>

Thomas' death was reported on 13 November 2020, aged 87.<ref>{{cite news |title=Sir John Meurig Thomas: Welsh scientist dies aged 87 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-wales-54939887 |access-date=13 November 2020 |work=BBC News |date=13 November 2020}}</ref>

== Awards and honours ==
Thomas held an Honorary Distinguished Professorship of Materials Chemistry at [[Cardiff University]].<ref name="RSHonours"/> He was an Advisory Professor at [[Shanghai Jiao Tong University]] and at the Catalysis Center of [[Hokkaido University]].<ref name="UIC2016">{{cite web |title=A Citation for Honorary Fellow Professor Sir John Meurig THOMAS |url=http://www1.uic.edu.hk/en/about-uic/570-english/other/20894-a-citation-for-honorary-fellow-professor-sir-john-meurig-thomas |website=United International College |access-date=30 April 2019 |date=14 June 2016 |archive-date=30 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430204923/http://www1.uic.edu.hk/en/about-uic/570-english/other/20894-a-citation-for-honorary-fellow-professor-sir-john-meurig-thomas |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was an Honorary [[Bencher]] of [[Gray's Inn]].<ref>{{cite web |title=This is a list of Honorary Benchers of Gray's Inn since 1883, when the Inn first used the title |url=https://www.graysinn.org.uk/sites/default/files/pictures/history/Honorary%20Benchers.pdf |website=Gray's Inn |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref>

Thomas received twenty-three honorary degrees<ref name="UIC"/> from Australian, British, Canadian, Chinese, Dutch, Egyptian, French, Italian, Japanese, Spanish, and U.S. universities, including an Honorary Degree of Doctor of Science from the [[University of St Andrews]] in 2012.<ref name="Wright">{{cite news |last1=Wright |first1=Paul |title=Laureation Address – Professor Sir John Meurig Thomas Friday |url=https://news.st-andrews.ac.uk/archive/laureation-address-professor-sir-john-meurig-thomas/ |access-date=30 April 2019 |work=University of St Andrews News |date=22 June 2012}}</ref> He was elected to honorary membership of over fifteen foreign academies, including the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] (2013),<ref name="IUPAC2013">{{cite journal |title=IUPAC 2013 Distinguished Women in Chemistry or Chemical Engineering / New Members of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition |date=23 September 2013 |volume=52 |issue=39 |pages=10154–10155 |doi=10.1002/anie.201305827 |bibcode=2013ACIE...5210154. }}</ref> the [[American Philosophical Society]] (1992), the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (1990),<ref name=":0"/>{{rp|xxii}} the {{lang|it|[[Accademia dei Lincei]]|italic=no}} (Rome, 2012),<ref>{{cite web |title=DETTAGLI DELLA MANIFESTAZIONE  |website=Accademia dei Lincei|url=http://www.lincei.it/modules.php?name=Convegni&file=lista&func=Convegni_scheda&Id=956 |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref> and the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] (1994).<ref name=":0"/>{{rp|xxii}} In 1993 he was elected an Honorary Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]].<ref name="FRSE1993">{{Cite news|url=https://www.rse.org.uk/fellow/john-thomas/|title=Sir John Meurig Thomas FRS HonFREng HonFRSE, FLSW|work=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|access-date=12 February 2018|language=en-GB}}</ref>

Other awards included the Kapitza Gold Medal from the Russian Academy of Natural Sciences (2011),<ref name="Angewandte"/> the Jayne Prize Lectureship of the American Philosophical Society (2011), the Bragg Prize Lectureship of the [[British Crystallographic Association]] (2010), the [[Sven Berggren]] Prize Lectureship, Lund (2010), the Ertl Prize Lectureship of the [[Max Planck Gesellschaft]] (2010), the [[Sir George Stokes Award|Sir George Stokes Medal]] from the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (2005),<ref name="Academia Europaea"/> the Giulio Natta Gold Medal from the Società Chimica Italiana (2004),<ref name=":0"/>{{rp|x}}  the Linus Pauling Gold Medal from [[Stanford University]] (2003),<ref name="Academia Europaea"/> and the [[American Chemical Society]] Annual Award (first recipient) for Creative Research in Heterogeneous and Homogeneous Catalysis (1999).<ref name=":0"/>{{rp|x}}  He won the [[Davy Medal]] of the [[Royal Society]]<ref name="RMAW"/> and the [[Faraday Lectureship Prize]] (1989) of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Faraday Lectureship Prize Previous Winners |url=https://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/FaradayLectureshipPrize/PreviousWinners.asp |website=Royal Society of Chemistry |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref> In 1995 he became the first British scientist in 80 years to be awarded the [[Willard Gibbs Award]] by the Chicago Section of the American Chemical Society.<ref>{{cite journal |title=WILLARD GIBBS AWARD |website=The Chemical Bulletin|publisher=American Chemical Society, Chicago Section|url=https://chicagoacs.starchapter.com/images/downloads/Chemical_Bulletin/2017_05_chembull.pdf |date=2017|issue=May|page=3 |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref> In 1967 he was a recipient of the [[Corday–Morgan Prize]].<ref name="To2013">{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/CordayMorganPrizes/PreviousWinners.asp|title=RSC Corday–Morgan Prize Previous Winners|publisher=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]]|access-date=9 October 2014}}</ref>

[[File:Meurigite-K-Ruifrancoite-109495.jpg|thumb|right|Yellowish-white hairy meurigite on brown ruifrancoite spheres]]
In recognition of his contributions to geochemistry, a new mineral, meurigite, was named after him in 1995 by the [[International Mineralogical Association]].<ref name="de Fourestier">{{cite journal |last1=de Fourestier |first1=J. |title=The Naming of Mineral Species Approved by the Commission on New Minerals and Mineral Names of the International Mineralogical Association: A Brief History |journal=The Canadian Mineralogist |date=1 December 2002 |volume=40 |issue=6 |pages=1721–1735 |doi=10.2113/gscanmin.40.6.1721 |bibcode=2002CaMin..40.1721D |s2cid=128701814 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/234007948 |access-date=29 April 2019}}</ref><ref name="Jambor">{{cite journal |last1=Jambor |first1=John L. |last2=Puziewicz |first2=Jacek |last3=Roberts |first3=Andrew C. |title=New Mineral Names |journal=American Mineralogist |date=1997 |volume=82 |pages=620–624 |url=http://rruff.info/doclib/am/vol82/AM82_620.pdf |access-date=29 April 2019}}</ref>
A hydrated potassium iron phosphate, meurigite is described as "tabular, elongated crystals forming spherical and hemispherical clusters and drusy coatings. The colour ranges from creamy white to pale yellow and yellowish brown."<ref name="Birch"/> It is found in only a few locations worldwide, of which the designated [[Type locality (geology)|type locality]] is the [[Chino mine|Santa Rita mine]] in [[Santa Rita, New Mexico|New Mexico]].<ref name="Birch"/>

Thomas's 75th birthday was celebrated at the University of Cambridge with a symposium and several musical and social events. It was attended by [[Angela Merkel]] and [[Ahmed Zewail]]. The papers presented were published in 2008 by the Royal Society of Chemistry as ''Turning Points in Solid-State, Materials and Surface Science: A Book in Celebration of the Life and Work of Sir John Meurig Thomas''.<ref name=":0"/>

In 2010 Imperial College Press published ''4D Electron Microscopy: Imaging in Space and Time'', which he co-authored with Ahmed Zewail (Nobel Laureate, Chemistry, 1999).<ref name="Hovmöller">{{cite journal |last1=Hovmöller |first1=Sven |title=4D electron microscopy – imaging in space and time, by Ahmed H. Zewail and John M. Thomas |journal=Crystallography Reviews |date=April 2011 |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=153–155 |doi=10.1080/0889311X.2010.520013 |bibcode=2011CryRv..17..153H |s2cid=97934253 }}</ref> His most recent publication is ''Design and Applications of Single-Site Heterogeneous Catalysts: Contributions to Green Chemistry, Clean Technology and Sustainability'' (2012)<ref name="Wells">{{cite journal |last1=Wells |first1=Richard |last2=McCue |first2=Alan |title=Design and Applications of Single-Site Heterogeneous Catalysts: Contributions to Green Chemistry, Clean Technology and Sustainability |journal=Platinum Metals Review |date=1 January 2013 |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=44–45 |doi=10.1595/147106713x660297 |url=https://www.technology.matthey.com/article/57/1/44-45/ |access-date=30 April 2019|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 2003, he was the first scientist to be awarded the Medal of the [[Honourable Society of Cymmrodorion]] (London) for services to Welsh culture and British public life.<ref name="Symposium"/> He was also a Founding Fellow of the [[Learned Society of Wales]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Yr Athro Syr John Meurig Thomas |url=https://www.learnedsociety.wales/fellow/john-meurig-thomas/ |website=The Learned Society of Wales |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref> and a Member of its inaugural Council.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wales gets a Learned Society to call its own |url=https://www.wales.ac.uk/en/NewsandEvents/News/General/WalesgetsaLearnedSocietytocallitsown.aspx |website=University of Wales |access-date=30 April 2019|date=25 May 2010}}</ref> From 2011 he was a member of the Scientific Advisory Committee for Wales.<ref>{{cite web |title=Internationally Respected Welsh Chemist to Speak at City Lecture |url=https://www.uwtsd.ac.uk/news/press-releases/press-releases-2014/internationally-respected-welsh-chemist-to-speak-at-city-lecture.html |website=University of Wales |access-date=30 April 2019 |date=1 April 2014 |archive-date=30 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430215234/https://www.uwtsd.ac.uk/news/press-releases/press-releases-2014/internationally-respected-welsh-chemist-to-speak-at-city-lecture.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was an overseer of the [[Science History Institute]] (Philadelphia), and a member of the International Advisory Board of the Zewail City of Science and Technology (Egypt).<ref>{{cite web |title=Supreme Advisory Board (SAB) |url=https://www.zewailcity.edu.eg/main/content.php?lang=en&alias=supreme_advisory_board_(sab_)_ |website=Zewail City of Science and Technology |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref>

Thomas was appointed as an Honorary [[Fellow]] of the [[Royal Academy of Engineering]] in 2013.<ref name=freng/> In 2016, he was conferred an Honorary Fellowship by Beijing Normal University-Hong Kong Baptist University United International College (UIC), in view of his distinguished achievements in catalysis and materials science, and his dedication and outstanding contributions to the popularisation of science.<ref name="UIC">{{cite web|website=United International College |url=https://web.uic.edu.hk/en/hfc/visits-and-activities/2096-uic-holds-8th-graduation-ceremony-and-honorary-fellowship-conferment|title=UIC holds 8th Graduation Ceremony and Honorary Fellowship Conferment|date=29 June 2016}}</ref>

In October 2016, the Royal Society awarded Thomas the [[Royal Medal]] for Physical Sciences "for his pioneering work within catalytic chemistry, in particular on single-site heterogeneous catalysts, which have had a major impact on green chemistry, clean technology and sustainability."<ref name="RMAW">{{Cite web |title=John Meurig Thomas |work= The Royal Society |date=2016 |access-date=25 September 2018 |url= https://royalsociety.org/people/john-meurig-thomas-12404/ }}</ref><ref name="RS2016">{{cite news |title=ARM technology creators among top scientists honoured by the Royal Society in 2016 |url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2016/07/top-scientists-honoured-by-the-royal-society/ |access-date=29 April 2019 |work=The Royal Society |date=19 July 2016}}</ref><ref name="LSW2016">{{cite news |title=Sir John Meurig Thomas awarded Royal Society's Royal Medal 2016 |url=https://www.learnedsociety.wales/royal-medal-2016/ |access-date=29 April 2019 |work=The Learned Society of Wales |date=27 July 2016}}</ref> [[Prince Andrew, Duke of York]] represented queen [[Elizabeth II]] at the ceremony.<ref name="Royal Medal">{{cite web |last1=Harris |first1=Kenneth |title=Royal Medal for Sir John Meurig Thomas |url=https://www.chemistryviews.org/details/ezine/9991391/Royal_Medal_for_Sir_John_Meurig_Thomas.html |website=Chemistry Views |access-date=30 April 2019|date= 23 October 2016}}</ref>

Also in 2016, the UK Catalysis Hub launched a new medal that "honours the achievements of Sir John Meurig Thomas, a distinguished professor in the field of catalysis."<ref name="JMT Medal"/> The JMT Medal will be awarded every year, to a person working in the United Kingdom, for outstanding achievement in catalysis or a closely related field.<ref name="JMT Medal">{{Cite web |title=JMT Medal |work=Catalysis Hub |date=2017 |access-date=25 April 2019 |url= https://ukcatalysishub.co.uk/jmt-medal/ }}</ref>
